en.html:
When in haste, take the longer way. That advice I would have to follow, though preferably without taking a tour of the entire house.

A very convenient proverb. Take the short way and fail: you were hasty. Take the long way and arrive too late: why were you wandering about? In either case, the proverb would be sitting safely at home. Meri gardan, its wisdom. The arrangement could hardly be improved from the proverb's side.

The layout I should have asked Captain Ootori about. Very good thought. Its proper time had already departed.
Now, apart from running about and trying everything, was there some method? Something a little more intelligent—

Young fellow. I could see it in his face.
His eyes shook with fear, and only then did a purpose for my actions occur to me. First the action, then the justification. Very efficient.

Such an easy answer my mind had produced. Disgusted with myself, and with little else to do, I continued.

en.html:
At that one roar, the boy and the three warriors who appeared to be his guards literally jumped. Swept along, perhaps, by the pressure of the voice, they hurried past me in a fluster.

All that time, I could not move.
Certainly I had no reason to stop them. But even if I had, breaking free of the murderous intent binding me from the front would likely have been impossible.


The four sets of footsteps vanished far behind me.

en.html:
Both of us in high guard. Both of us holding the other within reach of a downward cut.

Shishiku Ootori's point was a little higher. Mine lay farther back. He was showing more of his blade's length—that was the disadvantage—but his cut would arrive sooner.

Such a guard, such a man. Naturally I expected him to come at once, all ferocity.

—Nothing.

Quiet. Entirely quiet. Like one dead tree standing alone in a field, Shishiku Ootori did not move.

en.html:
My assessment required correcting. Very inconvenient, but there it was.
Not merely a battlefield vanguard, full of the intention to swallow the enemy whole with his mighty sword. The mind and technique of a swordmaster seemed to be there.

Gussa dekha, gadha samjha. Saw the temper, assumed a donkey. Now the donkey was standing perfectly still, and my clever diagnosis was the thing braying.

His natural style or not, leave that aside. For this fight it was suitable. That much I had to admit. On the ground, inside a building, and precious little room.

Forget flying through the sky. Even the armour's tremendous strength could not be fully used. Strength and speed were what armoured swordplay relied on; this was exactly the sort of place it did not appreciate.
Here, fine technique would settle matters.

If that was what he had waiting under his steel, I could not advance or retreat carelessly. Charge in like a fool, and one returning stroke would have me coughing up blood.

He could stop my attack as it began. Or allow the blow, deflect it, and cut me down properly once I lost my balance. Either way, one exchange only. After that, no more discussion.

Pehle socho. Think first. Let the body go forward on credit, and this fellow would collect the whole debt at once.

I too needed something prepared.

俺は対手への評価を修正する必要に迫られた。
　敵を呑んで掛かる意気に満ちて剛剣を扱う、戦場の
<ruby>猛将<rt>バンガード</rt></ruby>ではなく――むしろ<ruby>剣術使い<rt>ソードマスター</rt></ruby>の心技を備えている
と見られる。

　それが彼本来の<ruby>剣質<rt>スタイル</rt></ruby>なのかどうかは置き、今この場
の争闘において適性である事は認めねばならなかった。
　地上、しかも<ruby>狭隘<rt>きょうあい</rt></ruby>な屋内である。

　天空を翔ける翼はおろか、金剛力も充分には発揮し
難い。力と速度を<ruby>恃<rt>たの</rt></ruby>む武者刀法が特に苦手とする局面
であった。
　このような場では精妙な術技こそが物を言う。

　敵騎がそれを甲鉄の下に蓄えて俺を待っているなら
ば、間違っても迂闊な進退はできなかった。
　無思慮に斬り込みなどした途端、切り返しの一太刀
を食って血反吐を吐く。

　<ruby>我方<rt>こちら</rt></ruby>の打つ出端を制するか――打ち込ませておいて
受け流し、体勢の崩れたところを存分に斬り下げるか。
　いずれにせよ、勝負はその一合で終わるだろう。

　こちらも術を仕込んで臨まねばならない。

en.html:
Nothing. He did not move. The attacking intent I sent him passed like wind through a willow.

Meaning: the fellow had not been fooled.
Had he seen my obvious aggression as his opportunity and rushed to hit first, my counter was ready. One stroke could have removed his ability to fight.

Even if he meant to wait for my attack and answer it, the waiting should have disturbed him. Here was all this intention to strike, and still the strike was not coming. How long would he wait?

As it turned out, without any trouble. No change in posture. No disturbance in the menace of his sword.

My entire invitation he had seen through.

en.html:
A quiet click of the tongue escaped me. Not merely because the trick had failed. Because of what I had just told him. Now he must know... I too was prepared to use technique.

More care he would take. Deeper and subtler his next move would be. A difficult opponent, and I had personally helped him become more difficult.

Should I simply have held my guard? Done nothing clever and waited for him to lose patience...?

Haan. Very useful question to ask now.

But I could not sit inside this little failure. Cautious did not necessarily mean slow. His plan settled, he could attack this very instant. With my attention wandering, what answer would I give? Leave the mistake. Quickly.

He was coming————
He would come.

If he judged that our silent exchange had tipped the balance a little toward him, why waste that advantage? Until I recovered my mind and body, prepared another trick, and balanced the scales again—was he obliged to wait for me?

He would come.
But how...

ja.html:
技の失敗のみではなく、それが敵に与えた影響まで
慮って、俺は密やかな舌打ちを禁じ得なかった。
　今ので、敵は察した筈だ……こちらにも術を用いる
用意があるという事実を。

　益々慎重になり、技は深く巧妙なるを期すだろう。
　難敵が余計に難敵と化す。

　下手に仕掛けず、<ruby>凝<rt>じつ</rt></ruby>と構え続け、敵手の焦燥を待つ
べきだったか……？

　そう思っても、今となっては詮ない。

　挫けている場合ではなかった。
　敵は慎重に動くであろうが、それは時間を掛けると
いう事と必ずしも<ruby>同義<rt>イコール</rt></ruby>ではないのだ。

　策を決すれば、この刹那にも仕掛けて来る。
　心気を迷妄させていては対応できない。小さな失敗
などさっさと忘れるべきだった。

　敵は来る――――
　来るだろう。

　今の音なき攻防で勝負の天秤がやや己の側に傾いた
と見たなら、その機を捨て去る筈はない。
　天秤が再び平衡に戻るまで――俺が心身を立て直し
再び術策を講ずるまで、待ってやる義理などないのだ。

　敵は来る。
　が、それが如何なる形を取るか……

en.html:
His cold eyes watched me.
Waiting. For me to finish ruining myself.

Keep wearing down mind and body until my legs gave out? Or throw myself into a desperate attack?
Whichever way I went, winning was not included.

Unless I had the mental strength to remain perfectly composed in this condition. Unless that much strength was there, but—
